The caption explains that two free functions in the symmetry give two identities and two equations that follow from the others.|Fields against independent field equations]]

The second theorem's identities hold whether or not anything obeys the laws of
physics. This page asks what happens when something does.

== The answer is not a conservation law ==

For the first theorem, imposing the laws of physics turns an identity into a
conservation law. It is tempting to expect the same move to work here.

It does not. Imposing the laws of physics on a Noether identity gives you a
statement about the laws themselves: '''some of them follow from the others'''.

One free shape in the symmetry, one identity, one equation that was never
independent. The bookkeeping is exact.

== Describing a photograph ==

Suppose you describe a black-and-white photograph by giving a brightness number
for every point.

Now suppose the only thing anyone can ever see is '''contrast''' — differences in
brightness between neighbouring points. Add the same amount to every number and
the picture looks identical.

You have more numbers than you have picture. Exactly one number's worth of your
description carries no information, and no measurement will ever pin it down.
That is not a gap in your data. It is a feature of the description you chose.

Now allow yourself to add a different amount at each point, in a smooth pattern,
and still get the same visible picture. You have handed over a whole shape's worth
of description that means nothing, and the equations describing your picture will
have exactly one relation among them for each free shape.

That is the situation of every theory in modern physics that describes a force.

== The consequence for prediction ==

This has a sharp edge, and Hilbert put his finger on it in 1916 before the theorem
existed to explain it.

If some of your equations follow from the others, then knowing everything about
the present does not determine the future.

That sounds like a disaster and is not. What is undetermined is not anything you
could observe. It is the part of the description that was never carrying
information — the overall brightness in the photograph. Two futures that differ
only in that respect are the same future, described twice.

Hilbert stated the problem for his own scoring rule and spelled out the
consequence for prediction in his second paper. What he could not say, and what
the second theorem supplies, is that this is a general fact about local
symmetries rather than a peculiarity of one theory.

== The counts ==

For general relativity: four free shapes, one for each coordinate you are free to
relabel, so four identities and four equations that follow from the rest.

For electromagnetism: one free shape, one identity — and this is exactly why the
potentials of electromagnetism are not determined by the field equations, a fact
usually presented as a quirk of the subject rather than as an instance of a
theorem.

For the theories of the strong and weak forces, the counts are larger and the
principle is identical.

== Two things this does not say ==

'''It does not say the theory has too few equations.''' The number of equations
matches the number of physically distinct things exactly. It is the number of
'''variables''' that is larger than both, and it is larger on purpose, because
that is how a local symmetry gets written down.

'''It does not say the redundant equations are useless.''' They are true and they
are used constantly. They are simply not independent, and a physicist who counts
them as independent will conclude the theory is overdetermined when it is not.

== Why anyone would build a theory this way ==

The redundancy is not a price paid for some separate benefit. It '''is''' having
a local symmetry. Any theory with one has it, and every theory of a fundamental
force turns out to have one.

== What you do about it in practice ==

Since part of your description carries no information, you have to decide what to
do with the slack before you can calculate anything.

The usual answer is to make an arbitrary choice and write it down. Fix the overall
brightness of the photograph at some value and stop worrying about it. Physicists
call this '''fixing the gauge''', and it is one of the routine steps in setting up
almost any calculation about a force.

Two things about it are worth knowing.

The choice is genuinely arbitrary. Different choices are convenient for different
problems, and none is more correct than another. If two people make different
choices and compute the same observable quantity, they must get the same answer —
and if they do not, one of them has made a mistake, because a difference that
depends on the choice cannot be physical.

And the choice is not optional. Without it the equations do not determine a unique
answer, and a calculation that forgets to make one will run into that fact halfway
through, usually in a confusing form.
